questions.stem: Bruce, 74, is in ED with an upper GI bleed, probably from a peptic ulcer. He takes ibuprofen 400 mg TDS for hip and knee osteoarthritis and aspirin 100 mg daily since a stroke in 2013. He asks, "Can I keep taking my tablets?" Which explanation is best?
options: Stop both the ibuprofen and the aspirin for good, as together they caused the ulcer
Keep the ibuprofen, as long as you take the esomeprazole every day from now on
Stop the ibuprofen for good; aspirin may pause briefly but restarts within days
Change the ibuprofen to celecoxib and stop the aspirin until the ulcer has fully healed
questions.why: After an ulcer bleed the NSAID is stopped for good. Aspirin for secondary prevention after stroke is kept going or paused only briefly, then restarted within days once the bleeding is controlled, as agreed with gastroenterology, alongside a daily PPI.
notes: Stopping aspirin indefinitely leaves him without secondary stroke prevention, and his risk of a thrombotic event outweighs the risk of a rebleed once he is on a PPI.
A PPI lowers the risk but does not make continued NSAID use safe after a major ulcer bleed. The NSAID should be stopped and paracetamol used instead.
A COX-2 inhibitor still carries a risk of ulcer bleeding, and withholding aspirin for weeks until healing delays secondary stroke prevention without need.

questions.stem: Bruce, 74, has haematemesis and melaena. HR 116, SBP 106, Hb 84 g/L, platelets 268, INR 1.1, normal albumin and bilirubin, and only one spider naevus. The bleed is presumed non-variceal and endoscopy is planned within 24 hours. Which drug should you start now in the ED?
options: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g IV over 8 hours
Pantoprazole 80 mg IV, then an IV PPI continued until endoscopy
Terlipressin 2 mg IV every 4 hours until the bleeding is controlled
Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as prophylaxis against bacterial infection
questions.why: In a presumed non-variceal upper GI bleed, give a high-dose IV PPI (e.g. pantoprazole 80 mg IV) before endoscopy. Raising gastric pH helps keep the clot stable and reduces the high-risk stigmata that need endoscopic treatment.
notes: Tranexamic acid is not recommended in GI bleeding: HALT-IT showed no reduction in mortality and an increase in venous thromboembolic events.
Terlipressin is a splanchnic vasoconstrictor used for suspected variceal bleeding. Bruce has no evidence of portal hypertension.
Prophylactic antibiotics are given in variceal bleeding in cirrhosis to reduce infection and rebleeding. They are not indicated in a non-variceal bleed.

questions.stem: Bruce, 74, with haematemesis and 2 weeks of melaena, has a urea of 16.8 mmol/L (baseline 6.2) while his creatinine is 102 µmol/L (baseline 88). Apart from reduced renal perfusion, what mechanism best explains why the urea has risen much more than the creatinine?
options: Acute tubular necrosis from NSAIDs reducing tubular secretion of urea over several days
Catabolic stress response breaking down skeletal muscle protein to urea
Reduced hepatic urea production from alcohol-related liver injury
Blood protein digested in the gut, absorbed, then converted to urea by the liver
questions.why: Blood from an upper GI source is digested in the small bowel as a protein meal. The amino acids are deaminated and the liver converts the nitrogen into urea, so urea rises out of proportion to creatinine. Hypovolaemia adds a prerenal component.
notes: Acute tubular necrosis would raise creatinine substantially, and urea is filtered and reabsorbed rather than secreted. His creatinine has barely moved.
Stress catabolism adds little in a few hours and cannot explain a near-threefold rise. It is also not specific to an upper GI source.
Liver injury reduces urea synthesis, so it would lower urea, not raise it. Bruce's liver function is also essentially normal.

questions.stem: At gastroscopy, Bruce, 74, is found to have a deep ulcer on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum (duodenal bulb), with a visible vessel at its base. Erosion of which artery most likely caused his major haemorrhage?
questions.why: The gastroduodenal artery, a branch of the common hepatic artery, runs immediately behind the first part of the duodenum. Posterior duodenal bulb ulcers erode into it and cause brisk, life-threatening bleeding. Anterior ulcers are more likely to perforate.
notes: The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature of the stomach and bleeds from lesser-curve gastric ulcers, not from duodenal bulb ulcers.
The splenic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreas behind the stomach and can be eroded by posterior gastric ulcers, not by duodenal bulb ulcers.
The superior mesenteric artery passes in front of the third part of the duodenum, well away from the duodenal bulb.
